name: Silicone / onion extract scar gel (Mederma)

card.summary: OTC onion extract scar gel; trials found it no better than petrolatum.
card.note: Silicone products have somewhat more support than onion extract.

quick.overview:
Mederma is a popular OTC scar gel built around onion extract. Silicone gels and sheets are similar products.
Trials have generally not found it better than petrolatum.
quick.mechanism: Claimed to soften scars; a rabbit study found improved collagen organization without significant size reduction.
quick.risks: Safety data are limited; the product contains alcohol and fragrance.

chain: Gel is applied daily to a closed, healed scar
Hydrates the area and may influence collagen organization
Scar is meant to look softer and less raised
Less noticeable scar on the face or body
angle.text: Mederma is used on scars from surgery, acne and injuries with the goal of a smoother, less visible mark. Silicone gel and sheeting are the related approach with more published trial data on scar height, pigmentation and pliability [10][11].

lead: Mederma is an over-the-counter topical gel sold to make scars look softer, smoother and less noticeable; its signature ingredient is an extract of onion bulb (Allium cepa), and the listed active ingredient is allantoin [1]. People use it on healed surgical incisions, acne marks, and scars from cuts, burns and injuries once the wound has closed, aiming for a flatter, paler and less visible scar on the face or body. Silicone gels and sheets are the related class of topical scar products that dermatology reviews examine alongside it [14][10][11].

The brand was developed by Merz Pharmaceuticals and launched in the United States in 1997; it later passed to HRA Pharma (2019) and then to Perrigo [1][12]. Its manufacturer describes it as a leading doctor- and pharmacist-recommended scar brand in the United States, based on its own surveys, and says visible improvement can appear after about 8 weeks on new scars or 3 to 6 months on older ones [12].

Published research on onion extract is mixed. Small randomized trials compared the gel with petrolatum and reported no statistically significant difference in scar appearance, and a rabbit ear study found no significant reduction in scar size, height or inflammation but better organization of dermal collagen [1][2][3]. Systematic reviews of topical scar products describe a larger body of high-quality randomized trials for silicone gels and sheets than for onion extract, vitamin E or other products [14][10][11].

paras: Mederma is a water-based gel whose marketing says it can make scars softer, smoother and less noticeable [1]. Directions described for the flagship Advanced Scar Gel call for a thin layer applied once daily to a scar after the wound has closed and scabs and stitches have gone, massaged until absorbed, continued for weeks to months [12]. The brand line has grown to include an overnight cream, an SPF 30 scar cream, a gel for children aged two and over, a scar serum, reusable scar sheets, and a stretch mark lotion, according to a Grokipedia summary of the brand [12].

People reach for it for scars that are visible in daily life: surgical scars on the face, neck or torso, acne marks and healed injuries. In appearance terms the goal is a scar that is flatter, less red and closer to surrounding skin tone. Dermatology reviews group it with other over-the-counter scar products such as silicone gel, vitamin E and microporous tape [14].

Merz developed the product in the mid-1990s around an onion bulb extract and launched it in the United States in 1997 as an over-the-counter scar gel, according to a Grokipedia entry [12]. Wikipedia records that Merz owned the brand for more than 20 years before selling it to HRA Pharma in 2019, and that Perrigo acquired HRA in 2021; Grokipedia gives May 27, 2019 for the sale and April 2022 for completion of the Perrigo deal at roughly 1.8 billion euros [1][12]. Because the dates differ between sources, the acquisition year is best read as 2021 to 2022.

A 1998 Archives of Dermatology essay, Snake oil for the 21st century, discussed dermatology's long association with quackery and the direct-to-consumer promotion of skin products, and is part of the background literature on how skin products are marketed [8].

The marketed rationale is that onion extract, which contains flavonoids such as quercetin, influences fibroblast activity and collagen production in healing tissue, while the gel keeps the area moisturised [12]. Grokipedia also credits the extract with anti-inflammatory effects [12].

In the rabbit ear model of hypertrophic scarring, Mederma did not significantly reduce scar size, height or inflammation but was associated with improved dermal collagen organization compared with untreated scars; the authors described this as suggesting a possible effect on the formation of raised scars [1][2]. The study opened by noting that the product had become prevalent in clinical settings while little scientific evidence supported its use on hypertrophic scars [2].

A 1999 pilot trial found an onion extract gel less effective than petrolatum, and a 2006 prospective double-blinded study compared the gel with a petrolatum emollient on new surgical scars and reported no statistically significant difference [1][3]. A 2011 Los Angeles Times article cited by Wikipedia counted two randomized comparison trials with 38 participants in total, neither finding Mederma superior to petroleum jelly [1].

Other findings are summarised in Grokipedia, which should be read cautiously: a 2012 trial in post-surgical scars with a control showed significant improvement at 8 weeks, a split-scar study in 24 participants found no difference from petroleum jelly, a comparison in 45 burn patients found silicone gel sheeting outperformed onion extract gel, and a 2023 study in atrophic acne scars reported visible improvement at 14 days [12]. Critics cited in the same summary point to small, short and sometimes industry-funded trials, while the manufacturer's survey-based claims describe broad professional recommendation [12].

A 2020 systematic review of 34 trials of topical scar products (silicone gel and sheets, onion extract, vitamin E, trolamine and microporous tape) concluded that numerous high-quality randomized trials supported silicone gel sheets and gels, while a limited number of studies supported onion extract and the other products [14]. Wikipedia's hypertrophic scar entry says silicone gel sheeting may slightly improve appearance compared with onion extract, though whether it beats other methods is uncertain [4]. A 2023 systematic review of keloid treatments states that the literature supports silicone gel or sheeting together with corticosteroid injections as first-line therapy [10].

Silicone is the better-studied relative. A 2020 meta-analysis of six randomized trials with 375 patients found topical silicone gel lowered pigmentation, height and pliability scores on the Vancouver Scar Scale after surgery compared with placebo or no treatment, with gels and gel sheets comparably effective [11]. A separate comparative study examined silicones as nonocclusive topical agents, addressing the idea that silicone films work by blocking water loss from skin; it describes them as water-resistant yet permeable films [13].

Brand lines now overlap the two categories: Mederma sells reusable scar sheets alongside its onion extract gel, worn for many hours a day over weeks according to Grokipedia, and its creams contain dimethicone, a silicone [12].
The 2006 double-blinded study compared onion extract gel with petrolatum on new surgical scars [3]. The 2002 animal study used the rabbit ear model [2].

Registered trials include a 2012 post-surgical scar study of Mederma with 20 participants [5], a 2006 randomized comparison of two topical therapies for keloids and hypertrophic scars with 30 participants [6], and a 2019 study of 75 participants evaluating over-the-counter scar-management modalities [7].

Reviews: the 2020 systematic review of 34 trials found a stronger trial base for silicone products than for onion extract, and the 2020 meta-analysis of silicone gel in six trials reported significant improvements in scar height, pigmentation and pliability [14][11].

Mederma is sold for external use; its inactive ingredients include alcohol and fragrance, along with preservatives such as methylparaben [1]. Brand directions say to keep it away from the eyes and from open or damaged skin, that mild redness or itching can occur and usually resolves within days, that rare allergic reactions are possible, and that pregnant or breastfeeding users should consult a doctor [12].

Mederma is regularly mentioned in consumer scar-care discussions because it is widely stocked in pharmacies and priced around $20 to $40 per tube, according to Grokipedia, which also notes that critics compare its cost with petroleum jelly [12]. Its pharmacy-shelf visibility, together with a modest published trial base, makes it a recurring reference point in discussions of whether premium scar products differ from simple emollients and silicone sheeting [14][3].

Scar appearance is also addressed with silicone sheeting, corticosteroid injection for keloids, microneedling, lasers and sun protection of healing skin; reviews of these treatments are the usual place where onion extract gel is compared with alternatives [10][14].

lore.intro: Mederma is discussed in skincare and scar-care communities as the default pharmacy scar product, often alongside silicone sheets and petroleum jelly; the claims below are the brand's marketing positions and how research addresses them.

claims.claim: Mederma makes scars softer, smoother and less noticeable.
claims.believers: The manufacturer states this in its marketing and says visible improvement can appear in about 8 weeks on new scars [1][12]. Users who apply it daily often report gradual fading.
claims.experts: Two small randomized comparisons found no statistically significant difference from petrolatum [1][3]; a 2020 systematic review found limited trial support for onion extract [14].

claims.claim: Onion extract acts on collagen and fibroblasts to improve scar structure.
claims.believers: The brand rationale cites flavonoids such as quercetin influencing fibroblast activity and collagen production [12].
claims.experts: In the rabbit ear model, collagen organization improved while scar size, height and inflammation did not change significantly [2].

claims.claim: It is the leading doctor-recommended scar product.
claims.believers: The brand cites independent surveys of doctors and pharmacists [12].
claims.experts: Reviews of topical scar products emphasise silicone gel and sheeting as the best-supported over-the-counter option [14][10].

claims.claim: Silicone sheets outperform onion extract gels.
claims.believers: Scar-care discussions often recommend silicone sheeting for raised scars.
claims.experts: A 2020 meta-analysis of six trials found silicone gel lowered scar height, pigmentation and pliability scores [11]; Wikipedia notes sheeting may slightly improve appearance compared with onion extract [4].

claims.claim: Petroleum jelly does the same job for far less money.
claims.believers: Price comparisons in consumer discussion note the $20 to $40 per tube cost against a cheap emollient [12].
claims.experts: Trials found no difference between the onion gel and petrolatum on new surgical scars [3][1].

claims.claim: It can help older scars and stretch marks.
claims.believers: The brand says older scars may take 3 to 6 months and sells a stretch mark lotion [12].
claims.experts: No published randomized trial in the cited literature tests the gel on stretch marks; trials examined surgical scars and keloid or hypertrophic scars [3][6].
